newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SURVIVES FIVE SETTER AS HEAT TAKES TOLL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS SURVIVES FIVE SETTER AS HEAT TAKES TOLL.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras narrowly survived a five-set battle with a little-known Slovakian teenager, but Swiss prodigy Martina Hingis rarely looked in danger in fourth round matches at the Australian Open on Monday.
Dominik Hrbaty, a 19-year-old ranked 76 in the world, displayed the panache of a champion before Sampras reasserted himself to win 6-7 6-3 6-4 3-6 6-4 in two hours and 53 minutes.
"There's an old saying, it's better to be lucky than good and I definitely had a lot more luck than good today," Sampras told reporters after the match.
Hingis, the only leading seed left in the women's singles, had a few nervous moments in the first set against Romania's Ruxandra Dragomir before recovering to win 7-6 6-1 in 91 minutes.
The women's tournament has been depleted of top names after a weekend of upsets which saw world number one Steffi Graf and dumped out.

Hingis, the number four seed, is now installed as odds-on favourite to win the event and her next opponent will be another Romanian, eighth seed Irina Spirlea in the quarter-finals. Spirlea beat ninth seed Karina Habsudova of Slovakia 6-4 6-4.
"I just wanted to win this game and I was just so nervous, I don't know why," said Hingis.
"I just felt so different because it is a big grand slam tournament and there is a little chance to -- well, there is a big chance (to win)."
While Hingis maintained her composure, American 15th seed Chanda Rubin wilted on the second straight day of heatwave conditions at Melbourne Park.

Unseeded Belgian Dominique van Roost ended Rubins's run with a 7-5 6-4 victory, however American 14th seed Mary Joe Fernandez managed to keep her cool, recovering from a slow start to beat unseeded Swiss Patty Schnyder 4-6 6-4 6-1.
Third seed Goran Ivanisevic tapped into his last reserves of energy as his quest for a first grand slam title continued to build momentum.
Fighting back from two sets to one down, he hammered 38 aces on his way to beating unseeded Norwegian Christian Ruud 4-6 6-2 6-7 6-3 6-3 in match lasting over three hours.
Temperatures on Monday were even higher than at the weekend when they soared to 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) on the court.
"It was unbelievable I've never played in such conditions before," Ivanisevic said. "I was out of it, I didn't know where I was."
Ivanisevic will next meet Austrian fifth seed Thomas Muster who overcame a series of injuries to beat twice former Open champion Jim Courier 6-2 3-6 7-6 6-3.
Muster received treatment for shoulder and hip soreness and blistered toes during a match that lasted two hours and 42 minutes.
Sampras next faces Spanish 10th seed Albert Costa who had the easiest day, after eighth seed Wayne Ferreira of South Africa retired from their match with a leg injury.

After storming to victory on Saturday night, Sampras told reporters he would not even recognise Hrbaty if he bumped into him in the locker room -- although Hrbaty said he had asked Sampras for his autograph at the French Open three years ago.

After Monday's match, in which the teenager pushed Sampras around the court with long forehands and used a deep and powerful serve to whip up 20 aces, the Florida-based number one is unlikely ever to forget him.
"I think he believed he could beat me. I was very impressed," said Sampras. "I think he's going to be a player to be reckoned with in coming years."

The Slovakian is the youngest man in the top 100 and jumped 287 places in 1996 in the fastest rise of any player. He turned professional last year and has so far earned $71,000 compared to more than $25 million earned by Sampras.
Down 2-4 in the deciding set, Sampras looked to be in a daze, sapped of energy and heading for an upset loss rivalling his third-round exit at last year's Australian Open.

His tactic of conserving energy, waiting for the grand slam debutant to make mistakes, seemed at best risky as the teenager set pulses racing, earning a break point and a chance to serve for the match at 5-2.
Sampras saved the break point and, having closed out the game with an ace, his strategy finally began to pay off.
Hrbaty double-faulted in the next game to allow Sampras to even the score at 4-4 and then squandered another break point in the ninth game to lose his momentum entirely.
Sampras then shattered the Slovakian's dream of a grand slam quarter-final berth, breaking him in world number one style with a forehand winner down the line. REUTER
